59 Harvesttime, 79 A.V 

With the sudden declaration of the EMCAN, or the Erene Mankind Council Against Nekos, the Republic has made its deep offense to this organization clear, with a spoken condemnation by President Saradir, seconded by a written condemnation from the upper and lower houses of the Republic. "This organization is a sign that humanity has no intention of abandoning barbarism," Saradir told reporters on the 58th. "Hebasviriil will not participate in diplomacy with any organization committed to this council against the half-Ephemni in the Supreme Final Catgirl State."

In the formal condemnation written and issued by the  Archarecavai, Hebasviriil notes the history of humanity in limiting and oppressing non-humans, especially anthropomorphic individuals. It claims that the organization seeks only unity among human-supremacists to go against the International Court of Justice and once more massacre innocent sapients.

Any assets held by individuals from within the borders of the EMCAN are to be frozen until further notice, and foreign nationals within the country are demanded to leave as soon as possible. Hebasviriil hopes to resolve the situation diplomatically, though is adamant that no half-Ephemni or "catgirls" will die at the hands of humans if Hebasviriil has any say.

[quote=montfleur;61741098][b]September 7, 2028: The Aunt[/b]

There is much to be said about Madame Paolina, the most senior of the Paolinae family, she was a stout woman of wide proportions, seen by many as both a dame and a brute. Having been born in the age of the Nouveau Riche de Rosenmarkke, had granted her an air of independence which she used in a manner most liberal, and of which not one person dared to argue for.

Having been summoned by her niece-in-law following the infidelity scandal that had arisen with Iosep, she sought only to set the children right, though by her design she intended to wrest the poor wife and children away from Iosep, who she had disowned privately.

Moira dear, the humidity here is awful! Exclaimed Vita, I should wonder if one was really meant to live in such a region,

Moira Collete, a quiet and simpering woman merely nodded, her pale features aglow in the evening sunlight that poured through the windows of the upstairs sitting room, she had been crying, once again.

Where are the children? She asked, a question she had asked repeatedly throughout the evening.

They are with the nurse, although, I daresay they are getting old, why young Pietro is nearly fifteen! He should be at lacademie, replied Vita with a nod.

OhI wouldnt dare send him to such a severe place, he would perish, replied Moira.

Hardly my dear, many great officers have come from that place, 

Moira nodded, Well perhaps once this fiasco is over Ill look into it,

Money troubles my dear? Asked Vita, picking up what Moira had set down.

Oh heavens, I wouldnt dare say that!  lied Moira, shuddering at her lie.

Well, nevertheless, nevertheless, we shall set things to order, nodded Vita with resolve.

The door to the room opened suddenly with great energy as the eldest daughter Eliza ran into the room, her skirts flowing about her, she suddenly paused in the middle of the room realising her aunt was sitting there, curtsying politely she walked over to her mother, who smiled faintly.

Where have you been? Asked Moira.

I was out with the workers, replied Eliza.

The workers? Asked Vita, The farm workers? She harrumphed disapprovingly.

Yes, the grape harvest is almost ready, and wellI wanted to snatch some grapes! Replied Eliza.

Well did you bring me some? Asked Moira with a twinkle in her eye.

But of course! Laughed Eliza, opening her palm to reveal a bunch of grapes, And Aunt Vita can have some if she wishes!

Vita gave a firm no and merely said, How was the Fête with Anna?

It was enjoyable, the talk was a bit dry, all about politics and reunification, and there was a colonel there, an odd sort of man, began Eliza rambling.

Vita held up her hand, You are wandering dear, please, slow down, or Ill lose weight at this rate! She exclaimed with a cough.

You met a colonel? Asked Moira.

Yes, although I cannot remember his name, our conversation was brief, he offered me a ride home, 

Did you accept? Asked Vita.

Wellno, I mean a strange man asks you into his car at night, oh heavens, thats a death warrant waiting to be signed, replied Eliza.

She has a point Vita, even high society has dogs, sighed Moira as she remembered that her husband was one such animal.

What was his name? Asked Vita.

I do not recall, come to think of it, it was some sort of Montfleurois name, but frankly I could care less! Declared Eliza, Mama where is father?

Your father is in his study most likely, or with the lawyer in town, do remember dear we have a court date this week, replied Moira.

So Ill take Pietro and Madeline to the market on that day? 

Yes, I have no wish for those two to see the inside of a courthouse, and well, Madeline has to get ready for her coming out at Annas, 

Vita smiled, Moira, I was thinking perhaps Madeline would like to have her coming out party at the De Lorraines, 

Moira gave a startled look, The De Lorraines?! She exclaimed.

Yes, a suggestion by my daughter, Anna, she apparently met one of the nephews or some acquaintances of the president, replied Vita.

Well I am sure she would enjoy it, but, oh well she is so shy, and the people of that circle are usually so stiff, replied Moira.

Vita frowned, But they are the new people, and they are international! Which is the new way of things, 

Well Ill ask her about it, but nevertheless, I must go instruct the cook on dinner, Moira said, rising from her seat, Eliza please go check on Pietro, make sure hes done his arithmetic,

Eliza nodded and walked out of the room after hugging her aunt.[/quote]
[b]Dinner with the Collete family[/b]

The silverware shone dimly in the light of the candles which flickered gently in the dining room of the Collete home. Moira sat stiffly at the head of the table in a blue damask gown, beside her Vita in a matching skirt and blouse, and along the rest of the table the children, an empty seat at the far end of the table, half hidden in the shadows of the room lay empty.

Moira was about to remark about this, however the door to the room opened and Iosep stepped in, dressed in a slightly dirty dinner jacket, his hair unwashed, his beard untrimmed. Like a ghost he slipped into his chair, Moira cast her eyes down in a half nod half glance away.

Vita nodded silently and rang the little bell which sat on the table, a maid entered through the door, followed by another male servant laying out the first course, a cold consommé of goose.

Shall we pray? Asked Moira.

They did so, bowing their heads in solemnity and whispering some prayer, then the room filled with the click of spoons and gentle slurps of soup.

So, intoned Moira, setting the spoon down, How was everything today?

She smiled at her children and at Vita.

Eliza helped me with my Algebra, replied Pietro, Nasty stuff, he frowned.

Silence fell over the table once more.

Vita cleared her throat, Well, is it true that you are going to get your dress this week, Madeline? 

Madeline grinned, Yes! The dressmaker said itd be ready soon, oh mama, you should see it! She said excitedly.

Ispoke with the lawyer today, stuttered out Iosep.

Moira frowned, Did you? 

Yes, I think the court caseI think we should, he paused as Moira stared at him, Have you seen the priest? He asked, pivoting from the court discussion.

He is arriving tomorrow, replied Vita for Moira.

Ahyes, smiled Iosep grimly, I suppose I should clean up,

We will speak of this after dinner, she replied cooly as she waved the soup away for the next course.

Dinner continued in an awkward manner, low conversation, the clink of cutlery, a feeling of unease upon the room.

After dinner and the nightly tucking of the children, Moira made her way to her dressing room, seating herself before it and staring into the mirror. She looked pale, messy, her eyes were ringed with dark circles, the gray hairs she had spent the year hiding crept out boldly. 

A knock came at the door, she stiffened slightly and turned, listening for the voice, Moira? Enquired the voice, her lips tightened, it was her husband.

What do you want? She asked curtly.

Youwished to talk? 

I do not wish to talk any longer, she replied, turning to the mirror once more and trying on a pearl necklace.

Well, we must talk, replied Iosep, frustration rising in his voice.

What is there to talk about? Asked Moira her pitch rising.

There was a silence at the door, Moira frowned, rose, and opened the door to her husband, Well? She asked.

Iosep saw his wifes face, her state, and he slumped against the doorway, What have I done to this house? He asked her.

Moira did not move, planting herself firmly to keep him from entering the room, You chose this,

But I regret it! Declared Iosep, I have been faithful to you for this decade! What has led to this tragedy but a moment of weakness!

Youyou led to this moment of weakness! Cried Moira, And now I, and this family, and my children, have been thrown into hell! 

And I am terribly sorry, declared Iosep, sliding to the ground.

Moira clung to the door frame as she stared down at the crying wreck that had been her husband, Leave, she stated, There is nothing to speak about, you yourself have confirmed your crime, I will seek to save my dignity and my children, 

Iosep looked up at his wife, Is there something that can be done? 

Done?! Declared Moira, The only thing that can be done is you signing those d-mned papers you have been running back and forth with the lawyer! Give me my fair share, and depart! 

She stepped back from the door and prepared to close it, Now go, clean yourself up, and for once in your life, act like a man! As far as I am concerned, when I am gone, you can sodomise yourself across the entire country! She shut the door with a firm click and walked into her bedroom, where a maid sat quietly waiting to help her into her slip. 

Iosep sat silently outside the door, tears running down his face. Quietly standing up, he brushed himself off, listened to hear if she was speaking anymore, and then walked downstairs to his office once more.

[i]The Velnaz Times presents a special article today -authored by one of our top journalists, who toured an Andrudin demonstration to get the "Word on the Ground":[/i]

Andrudin has long been the pulse of Stani culture, politics, and the first in line to make changes. Originally one of many small townships that dotted the Sunthorn river, the 1800s saw rapid industrialization and urbanization. Despite being the nation's youngest city, it carries scars and memories of a troubling past.
The birth of Andrudin as more than a middle-of-nowhere river village was tumultuous. Mill Families staffed their facilities with poor citizens from the Dniezhidnov Territory, Ystwlsi and Sverdraugh people who couldn't afford the taxes being imposed to keep the mills afloat. Women and children were forced to work and die for pennies a day, and the City revolted. The Crown retaliated, sending in Private-ish militias and establishing the practice that many others had adopted- maintaining a national guard. The Crown outlawed the Ystwlsi language in 1807 inside of the city, and removed it from public school curricula the nation over. The back and forth between the workers and the Crown continued until 1890, during the 3 long years that nearly leveled the city. The New Republic promised hope and saftey, until it was seized by so-called "Democratic Republicans", who removed the workers party entirely, and instituted an Apartheid government that placed Kyraniyans and Greeks at the top, Ystwlsi and Elven Lokaeans as subhuman.

The "Decolonize" demonstration there had a big turnout, cheerful protesters chatted with the cities law enforcement, whose off and on-duty members were present in support of the demonstrations. The Andrudin Mayor, as well, spoke at the rally. Whilst there, I had interviewed a young man, well-spoken, and one of many important voices to hear:
[list][sub]Me (I): "So, what are the aims of the demonstration today?
He (H): "Ah, well, to get an audience. The best way to make change is be heard, and we've the right to be heard."
"Well I write for a paper, what do you want heard today?"
"This is the first step, check the Neu-Stalsi manifesto, we have our steps laid out: Organize, get attention, organize more, strike, strike again, and appeal to the international sensibilities.

The Queen is far away from the Republican Apartheid state, she hated it. I trust we can be heard, ah?"

"So when you say Decolonize now?"

"Home rule, concentrated power and dictatorship, in the real sense of dictatorship, at a manageable jurisdiction. Some call them soviets, counsels, districts- Stalsi speaking for Stalsi, ya?"

"Are the Neu-Stalsi seeking an independent state?"

"Some. I can't speak for them, I understand the value of a large infrastructure, but the way we want to do things now- confusing Nation for Country, its the old ways continued, Patriarchy and Capital spinning us like a top. I think we have a unique oppurtunity here, in this land specifically, to change the way of things."

"These are some 'Revolutionary' thoughts, no?"

"Yes, they are. This is some revolutionary time. We can't stop because things are good, we owe it to ourselves to continue what we started. I [i]know[/i] what our flag and revolution stand for. It's this exact thing, over and over until it's perfect.

[/sub][/list]

Veronika, Susana, and Red sat around a small table in one of the upstairs rooms. Elena had been at the coast for several days, with no word from Cecilia nor Marniy. Red and Zana played a game of chess, Nika smoked cigarette after cigarette. Smoke filled the room, butts filled the ashtray, and the fan in the window was working overtime.

Red moved a pawn, "See the times today?"

Zana nodded. "Decolonizing. We've been busy at the IAM working on Vočes Popêlizdat. Round the clock, meetings with informants, foreign government leaders, recommendations for really good proletariat education programs. The problem comes with Federating the Empires authority and making sure it works out. Hand over absolute power and this thing could give out on us."

Red thought for a moment. "Well, yeah. All at once would be impossible, if not stupid. Is VP supposed to be a governing structure?"

Zana shook her head, "Not at first, but what will they push for? Radicals are seldom predictable, you know."

"That's where the strength of a country comes from. You read the article, nations and countries are different beasts. Sorry I can't chat longer," he stood from his chair,

"I have a meeting with the President of Cieskahlia, things are looking ugly in the west."
